FLASHCARD SET · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Home and Daily Life flashcards.

A house is a child’s first country, and this set is its phrasebook. Forty-one cards walk the whole home — the rooms and their furniture, the wash-and-get-ready routines, the kitchen verbs, the chores and the toolbox, the mail by the front door, the sounds the house makes when nobody is watching, and the green habits that keep it all running. The cards speak the everyday words of the US, UK and Canada — and where the countries differ (the tap and the faucet, the torch and the flashlight, the trolley and the cart), both words ride along, so every family hears its own home talking.

HOW TO USE THESE CARDS

Four ways that work.

You do not need a plan or a printer schedule. Pick one idea, try it for two minutes and see what happens.

  1. 01

    The house hunt

    Call a word from the cards — "sink!" "cushion!" "doormat!" — and your child runs to touch the real thing. Every room of your actual home becomes the answer key, and the sprinting burns each word in deep.

  2. 02

    Same home, two words

    The cards quietly carry both flavors of English: tap and faucet, torch and flashlight, wardrobe and closet, trolley and shopping cart. Point and say both — your child picks a favorite, or keeps both like secrets.

  3. 03

    One card, one room

    Stick the bedroom card on the bedroom door, the bathroom card by the sink, the kitchen card on the fridge. The word lives where the thing lives, and reading the room becomes reading the words.

  4. 04

    The tidy-up draw

    The cleaning, storage and laundry cards make a tidy-up team: draw one at random and do that job together for five minutes. The vacuum cleaner card gets requested first, every time.

      Rooms at Home Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Rooms of the home

      The rooms-at-home card shows the five rooms a house is made of — the bedroom, the kitchen, the bathroom, the living room and the garden — each one drawn in its own little window of the card.

      Say it together

      “Rooms at home! Here is the bedroom where we sleep, the kitchen where we cook, the bathroom where we wash, the living room where we play — and the garden! Some families call the garden the yard. Both are right.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play "which room?" — say a room name and let your child run to the real one. Five rooms, five dashes across the house, and every name lands somewhere your child already lives.

      Quick parent note

      Room names are usually a child’s first map words — words that say where things are. Ask "which room is the kettle in?" and the map starts working on its own.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Rooms at Home lesson on the Learning Path.

      Parts of the Home (Inside) Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Rooms of the home

      This card names the parts every home is built from on the inside — the window, the door, the stairs, the wall and the floor — the pieces your child touches every day but may never have been told the words for.

      Say it together

      “Parts of the home! The window lets the light in. The door opens and closes. The stairs go up — step, step, step. The wall holds the house up, and the floor is what we stand on.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Go on a parts hunt: touch one window, one door, one wall and one floor without leaving the hallway. The stairs get a grown-up hand and a slow count of every step.

      Quick parent note

      Naming the fixed parts of a home hands a child the words for directions and safety at once: hand on the rail, feet on the floor, close the door gently. The vocabulary quietly does the supervising.

      Teach it, step by step

      Parts of a Home (Outside) Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 4–5Rooms of the home

      Walk around the outside and a home shows its other parts — the front door, the windows, the roof, the chimney and the garage — all the pieces you can point at from the sidewalk.

      Say it together

      “Parts of a home — outside! The front door is where guests knock. The roof sits on top like a hat. Smoke used to drift out of the chimney, and the car sleeps in the garage.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Stand at the curb and count the parts together: one roof, one front door — how many windows? The houses on your street become a counting game with names.

      Quick parent note

      Some homes have no garage and some have no chimney — say that too. "Some homes do, some homes don’t" is one of the most useful sentences a young child can hear.

      Teach it, step by step

      Living Room Words Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Rooms of the home

      The living-room card names the room where the family gathers: the sofa, the television, the coffee table, the floor lamp and the remote control — five words for the room your child already knows best.

      Say it together

      “Living room words! We sit on the sofa, the lamp glows in the corner, and the television lives on its stand. Who has the remote control? Not under the coffee table again!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play sit-and-name: from the sofa, name five things you can see, then swap seats and name five more. The living room turns out to be full of words that were hiding in plain sight.

      Quick parent note

      The remote control is the label everyone loves. Hand it over and say "the remote turns the television on" — one word for the object, one sentence for what it does.

      Teach it, step by step

      Furniture Words Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Rooms of the home

      Furniture is the word for the big things in a home that stay put — the armchair, the bookshelf, the rug, the cabinet and the stool — and this card names five of them at once.

      Say it together

      “Furniture words! An armchair is a chair with arms for hugging. A bookshelf holds the stories. The rug is soft under bare feet. The cabinet keeps the dishes, and the stool is just the right size for you.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Furniture you can feel is furniture you remember: sit on the chair, kneel on the rug, stand on the stool (with a hand nearby). Then ask "which furniture do books love best?"

      Quick parent note

      In the UK a cabinet is often called a cupboard — same piece of furniture, friendlier word. Offer both names and let your child keep the one that fits your kitchen best.

      Teach it, step by step

      Bedroom Words Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Rooms of the home

      The bedroom card names the room’s own furniture: the bed, the pillow, the blanket, the wardrobe and the bedside table — everything a good night needs, in five words.

      Say it together

      “Bedroom words! The bed holds you, the pillow holds your head, the blanket holds the warm in. The wardrobe keeps your clothes — some families say closet — and the bedside table keeps your water and your book.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Tonight, name all five as they happen: pillow fluffed, blanket up, book on the bedside table, light off. Bedtime runs smoother when every step has a name.

      Quick parent note

      Wardrobe and closet are the same friend wearing different name tags — pick whichever your family says, or teach both and let your child enjoy knowing a second word nobody asked for.

      Teach it, step by step

      Bedroom Objects Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Rooms of the home

      More from the bedroom: the bed and the lamp, the curtain, the rug and the alarm clock — the small objects that turn a room into your child’s own room.

      Say it together

      “Bedroom objects! The lamp makes a little pool of light. The curtains close the day. The rug is warm for bare feet in the morning, and the alarm clock says good morning even before you do.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hand over the two switches that matter: your child opens the curtains in the morning and clicks the lamp on at story time. Owning the light is owning the mood of the room.

      Quick parent note

      An alarm clock is also a first clock. Point at it: the short hand is on the seven — that is when we wake. Numbers hiding inside everyday objects are free lessons.

      Storage Words Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Rooms of the home

      Storage is the home’s quiet magic — the drawer, the cupboard, the shelf, the basket and the box — the five homes-for-things that give everything a place to live.

      Say it together

      “Storage words! Socks live in the drawer, dishes in the cupboard, books on the shelf, toys in the basket — and the box can hold anything at all. Even another box, one day.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play where-does-it-live with five real things: a spoon, a teddy, a book, a sock, a crayon. Every correct home gets a cheer — and tidy-up time quietly starts running on this game.

      Quick parent note

      Cupboard is the UK favorite; American families often say cabinet or closet. Whichever word your home uses, the idea is the same and worth saying often: everything has a home, just like everyone.

      Household Objects Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Rooms of the home

      The things that make a house feel like yours: the clock, the picture frame, the vase, the cushion and the curtain — the soft, small, everyday objects this card calls household objects.

      Say it together

      “Household objects! The clock ticks, the picture frame holds someone we love, the vase holds the flowers, the cushion holds your head on the sofa, and the curtain holds the whole day out at bedtime.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Ask what the clock says right now — any answer is a good one, because the game is noticing the object, not reading the time yet. Then find the frame with your favorite person in it.

      Quick parent note

      Cushion and throw pillow name the same soft thing on different sides of the Atlantic. Household words travel well between countries — point at yours and use the word your family likes.

      Daily Routines Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Wash and get ready

      The daily-routines card walks one whole day in five steps: wake up, get dressed, eat breakfast, brush teeth and go to bed — the same order every day, and that sameness is exactly the point.

      Say it together

      “Daily routines! We wake up, we get dressed, we eat breakfast, we brush our teeth — and at the very end of the day, we go to bed. The day has a shape, and you already know it!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Draw the five steps as a little chart and let your child move a clothespin from step to step as the day happens. The child who runs the routine almost never fights it.

      Quick parent note

      Routines are how young children tell time before they can read a clock. After breakfast we brush teeth means more than at eight o’clock ever will.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Daily Routines lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Home and Daily Life (Extra Class) room — with every lesson one tap away.

      Bedroom Routines Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Wash and get ready

      The bedroom, morning and night: make the bed, open the curtains, get dressed, read a book and turn off the light — the bedroom routines that bookend the whole day in one room.

      Say it together

      “Bedroom routines! In the morning we make the bed and open the curtains — hello, day! At night we read a book and turn off the light — goodnight, room.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      A made bed is a big job done small: pillows first, blanket up, finished. Let your child own the whole sequence every morning — wobbly corners and all — and the pride repeats daily.

      Quick parent note

      The bed is the day’s first and last task. Children who make their own bed learn that finishing something feels good — a lesson the rest of the day gets to borrow.

      Bathroom Words Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Wash and get ready

      The bathroom card names the room’s five big friends: the sink, the bath, the shower, the towel and the soap — everything wash day needs, drawn and labeled on one card.

      Say it together

      “Bathroom words! Water comes out of the sink, the bath fills up nice and deep, the shower goes pssh from up high. The soap makes bubbles and the towel waits, warm and fluffy.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Name each one at bath time as it happens: soap on, water running, shower pssh, towel out. The bathroom is the vocabulary room — every single night is the lesson.

      Quick parent note

      The tap has a second name across the ocean: Americans call it the faucet. Both words are welcome in your bathroom — the sink does not mind, it only cares that hands get washed.

      Teach it, step by step

      More Bathroom Words Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Wash and get ready

      The rest of the bathroom: the bath mat, the mirror, the toothbrush holder, the toilet and the toilet paper — the everyday words every child needs for the room they use most.

      Say it together

      “More bathroom words! The mat keeps wet feet safe, the mirror shows your shiny teeth, the toothbrushes stand in their holder — and yes, the toilet and the toilet paper. Everybody uses them!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Mirror games: brush teeth watching the mirror, then make a happy face, a surprised face and a sleepy face. The mirror turns tooth-brushing into a show with an audience of one.

      Quick parent note

      Toilet words are body words — say them plainly, without a giggle, and they stay that way. A child who can name everything calmly can ask for help calmly too.

      Teach it, step by step

      Bathroom Routines Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Wash and get ready

      The bathroom in action: wash hands, brush teeth, wash face, take a bath and dry hands — five routines, one room, every single day, all in order on one card.

      Say it together

      “Bathroom routines! Wash hands with bubbles, brush teeth up and down, wash face — brrr, tickles! Take a bath, then dry hands on the towel. All clean!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Give each routine its own two-line song: one for hand washing, one for teeth. The same songs every time turn routines into music your child starts without being asked.

      Quick parent note

      Drying hands is the forgotten half of washing. Hands get their own towel, the child gets the job — and the last step of the routine belongs entirely to them.

      Teach it, step by step

      Washing & Bathing Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Wash and get ready

      Bath night, item by item: the shower gel, the sponge, the bath towel, the bath toys and the hair dryer — the washing-and-bathing words that make the tub feel like an adventure.

      Say it together

      “Washing and bathing! Squirt the shower gel, scrub with the sponge — bbbrrr! — and when the bath is done, the towel wraps you up like a hug. The toys helped the whole time.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Give the toys their own wash day: teddy gets the sponge, ducky gets a rinse, the boat dries on the edge. A child who washes a doll’s hair sits far more still for their own.

      Quick parent note

      The hair dryer is a grown-up tool — warm air, never hot, and always held by a parent. Name it, let them press the cool button once, keep the hot part to yourself.

      Personal Care Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Wash and get ready

      Taking care of yourself, item by item: the toothbrush, the toothpaste, the hairbrush, the comb and the tissue — the personal-care words that go with growing up proud.

      Say it together

      “Personal care! The toothbrush and toothpaste keep your smile strong, the hairbrush and the comb make your hair behave, and the tissue is there for any nose that needs it.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Run the two-minute toothbrush timer, then ask which one is next — your child names and picks: brush, paste, hairbrush. Owning the order is half the battle won.

      Quick parent note

      A soft brush for teeth, a wide-tooth comb for tangles, and one rule with teeth: these tools are yours alone. Personal care is personal — nobody borrows a toothbrush.

      Teach it, step by step

      Kitchen Actions Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+In the kitchen

      The kitchen is a room of verbs: cook dinner, set the table, wash dishes, open the fridge and pour a drink — five actions that turn watching dinner happen into helping it happen.

      Say it together

      “Kitchen actions! We cook dinner on the stove, set the table — plate, cup, spoon — wash the dishes after, open the fridge for the milk, and pour a drink. The kitchen is where things get done.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Give one real action each evening: set the table, pour the water, or stir the pot from a stool with a grown-up beside. Verbs need a child’s hands to stick.

      Quick parent note

      Fridge is short for refrigerator — both words are correct and both are fun to say. Action words like cook, set, wash and pour are the grammar of helping.

      Teach it, step by step

      Home Appliances Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+In the kitchen

      The helpful machines of home: the television, the fan, the computer, the toaster and the iron — five appliances, each with its own job and its own rules.

      Say it together

      “Home appliances! The television shows the cartoons, the fan goes whirr on hot days, the toaster pops the toast — pop! — and the iron and the computer are grown-up machines we treat gently.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Appliance sounds: whirr, pop, beep. Ask which machine makes which sound and hunt the house for it. Sound games teach the object faster than the picture does.

      Quick parent note

      The toaster is the perfect first appliance: visible, quick, and its result is delicious. With a grown-up, watch the bread go in, count to the pop — toast happens.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Home Appliances lesson on the Learning Path.

      Shopping Words Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 4–5In the kitchen

      The shopping trip in five words: the shopping bag, the basket, the receipt, the wallet and the trolley — the words that turn coming along into helping.

      Say it together

      “Shopping words! We carry the shopping bag, fill the basket, pay from the wallet, keep the receipt — and push the trolley. In America they say shopping cart — same wheels, same fun.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Next shop, hand your child a picture list: apples, bread, soap. Finding three real things is a reading game the whole store plays along with.

      Quick parent note

      Trolley and cart roll through this card on purpose — families in the US, UK and Canada all shop, and both words are right. Your child can be bilingual in groceries.

      Cleaning & Tidying Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 3+Chores and tools

      The cleaning kit: the sponge, the cloth, the spray bottle, the bin and the vacuum cleaner — five words that make tidy-up time feel like having real tools of the trade.

      Say it together

      “Cleaning and tidying! The sponge soaks up spills, the cloth wipes the table, the bin eats the rubbish — Americans say trash — and the vacuum cleaner goes vrrrooom across the floor.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      A small spray bottle with only water inside, plus a cloth, is the table-wiping job children request forever. Give the tools real jobs and the chores start asking for themselves.

      Quick parent note

      Bin, trash can, garbage can — three countries, one important job. Whatever your word, the rule travels with it: what goes in the bin stays in the bin.

      Teach it, step by step

      “Cleaning tools! The broom sweeps — swish, swish. The mop washes the floor wet and clean. The bucket carries the water, the dustpan catches the crumbs, and the duster tickles the shelves.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      A child-size broom or a personal dustpan turns floor crumbs into a job your child fights to own: crumb hunt — sweep, catch, tip into the bin, cheer.

      Show each tool its one job: brooms sweep, mops wet-wash, dusters tickle. Tools with one clear job are easier to use correctly than the-cleaning-thing.

      Laundry Words Flashcard for Preschoolers

      Ages 4–5Chores and tools

      Where clothes go to get clean: the washing machine, the detergent, the clothesline, the clothespin and the iron — the laundry words for the whole journey, dirty to folded.

      Say it together

      “Laundry words! The washing machine tumbles the clothes round and round with the detergent making bubbles. On sunny days the clothesline hangs them out, held by clothespins, and the iron smooths the wrinkles away.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Load the machine together — colors sorted, detergent measured by the grown-up, counting done by the child, start pressed together. Then peg two socks on a rope at home for a mini clothesline.

      Quick parent note

      Clothesline and clothespin are the American pair; British families say washing line and pegs. The washing machine itself is the star — round and round, hypnotic and useful at once.

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      One bucket, one sponge, one very patient car: washing the car is the classic first chore because the water is the reward. Leaves get piled — jumping in first, bagging second.

      Quick parent note

      Feeding the birds comes with its own manners: morning, quiet voices, gentle hands. Chores that care for something smaller than you are empathy practice wearing overalls.

      “Garden tools! The shovel digs big holes, the rake gathers the leaves — rrrike. The trowel is the shovel’s little cousin for small hands, the gloves keep the dirt off, and the wheelbarrow carries it all.”

      Try this

      Hand your child the trowel and one pot: digging one small hole is a complete, proud job. Gloves on first — that little ritual is what makes the rest feel official.

      Quick parent note

      Every tool here has a one-job rule: shovels dig, rakes gather, trowels plant. The wheelbarrow is the reward — a ride in it is the best seat in the whole garden.

      Try this

      A ruler is the friendliest tool in the box: measure everything this week — shoes, spoons, the cat, if the cat allows. Measuring is math wearing overalls.

      Quick parent note

      Pointy things point down, and tools never leave the toolbox without a grown-up. Say it the same way every time and the rule becomes furniture in the child’s head.

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Build a by-the-door spot together: one hook for the coat, one basket for the shoes, one hook for the umbrella. Leaving the house becomes a checklist your child can run.

      Quick parent note

      The doormat has a job — wipe, wipe, wipe — and it saves the floors on every outing. Keys are grown-up treasure: they live up high and never, ever get played with.

      First-aid box and first-aid kit are the same brave little box with two names. And the keys stay up high and out of play — the rule comes attached to the word, every single time.

      “Home safety! The smoke alarm beeps to warn us. The torch — Americans say flashlight — lights up the dark. The safety gate keeps little ones off the stairs, and the fire extinguisher and reflective vest wait for the grown-ups.”

      A smoke alarm is a friend with a loud voice — say so long before it ever beeps for real. And safety tools are like tools everywhere: grown-ups use them, children know them.

      Try this

      Appoint the energy police for one day: who spots a light on in an empty room? Who turns the tap off while brushing? Little officers, big savings, endless pride.

      Quick parent note

      Water and energy are the home’s two treasures, and this card makes saving them a game instead of a scolding. The plug stays a grown-up thing — said with the word, every time.
